lead: An argument is a set of statements where some, the premises, are offered as reasons for another, the conclusion. The argument is valid when the conclusion cannot be false while every premise is true. Checking that row by row in a truth table is slow, so logicians give names to a small set of argument forms that are always valid: modus ponens, modus tollens, and a handful more. A proof is then a numbered chain in which every line is a premise or follows from earlier lines by one named rule. Programmers meet this in program verification, in Prolog, and in every bug report that must name one cause.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for connectives and truth tables, and 1.2 for tautologies and the contrapositive.

blocks.text: An argument is a set of statements. The premises give the reasons; one conclusion is the claim they support. We write P₁, P₂, …, Pₙ ⊢ C, where the symbol ⊢ is read "therefore". Take: "If the server is down, UPI payments fail. UPI payments failed. Therefore the server is down." Its shape is q, p→q ⊢ p.

An argument is valid when no situation makes all the premises true and the conclusion false. Validity is about form, not about whether the premises happen to be true in the real world. A valid argument whose premises are all true is called sound. Swap Chennai for any other city in a valid form and it stays valid.
P₁ ∧ P₂ ∧ … ∧ Pₙ → C is a tautology
blocks.where: P₁ to Pₙ are the premises, C is the conclusion, ∧ means and, → means implies. The argument is valid exactly when this one formula is true in every row of its truth table.

blocks.text: With k propositional variables the truth table has 2^k rows. Hunt for a single row where every premise is true and C is false. If no such row exists, the argument is valid (this is the tautology test of 1.1). Two rules carry most of the work. Modus ponens (MP): from p and p→q infer q. Modus tollens (MT): from ¬q and p→q infer ¬p. MT applies modus ponens to the contrapositive: p→q is equivalent to ¬q→¬p, so from ¬q we get ¬p (see 1.2).
Each row below is a small valid argument form. You can confirm any row with a truth table once, then use it by name forever. p, q, r, s are propositions.

How to read it

blocks.text: Addition looks odd: from "it is raining" you infer "it is raining or the bus is late". The conclusion is weaker than the premise, and a weaker statement is never false when the stronger one is true. The two dilemmas are just case splits — the constructive one says: the world is in case p or in case r; p forces q and r forces s; so q∨s holds either way.

A formal proof is a numbered column. Every line is either a premise or a formula obtained from earlier lines by exactly one named rule, and the last line is the conclusion. Nothing is written because it "looks obvious".

items: Write the formula on that line.
Write the justification: the word premise, or a rule name plus the line numbers it was applied to.
Stop when the required conclusion appears; the proof is complete.

blocks.text: Two look-alike patterns are invalid and appear in exams every year. Affirming the consequent: from q and p→q, inferring p. Denying the antecedent: from ¬p and p→q, inferring ¬q. Both fail because p→q tells you nothing when p is false. Let p be "the power is cut" and q be "the room is dark": the room can be dark at night with power on, so q with p→q does not give p.

Of the rules that use one implication together with one of its parts, only MP (from p) and MT (from ¬q) are valid. HS, CD and DD are also valid, but combine two implications or add a case split. Machines use a single rule, resolution, instead of all nine; that is the subject of 1.9.

figure.caption: Two applications of modus ponens carry p to r: p with p→q gives q, and that q with q→r gives r. Every other block is a premise taken as given.

examples.question: The premises are p→q, q→r and p. (a) Prove r with a numbered formal proof, naming the rule used at every line. (b) Confirm validity by counting: how many rows does the truth table have, how many rows make all three premises true, and how many of those rows make r false?
steps: Line 3: q — modus ponens on lines 1 and 2.
Line 5: r — modus ponens on lines 3 and 4. This is the conclusion, so the proof ends.
Part (b). Three variables p, q, r, so the truth table has 2³ = 8 rows.
Keep only rows where p is true: 4 rows. In each of those, p→q forces q = T, which leaves 2 rows (q = T, r still free).
With q = T, q→r forces r = T, so exactly 1 row satisfies all three premises, namely p = T, q = T, r = T.
In that row r is true, so the number of rows with all premises true and r false is 0.
examples.answer: r follows from p and q by two applications of modus ponens; the truth table has 8 rows, exactly 1 satisfies all premises, and 0 of those make r false, so the argument is valid.
examples.check:
from itertools import product
rows = list(product([True, False], repeat=3))
def ok(p, q, r):
    return p and (not p or q) and (not q or r)
sat = [t for t in rows if ok(*t)]
print(len(rows))
print(len(sat))
print(sum(1 for t in sat if not t[2]))

traps: Affirming the consequent (q, p→q ⊢ p) and denying the antecedent (¬p, p→q ⊢ ¬q) are invalid. They are the examiner's favourite distractors; of the rules that use one implication together with one of its parts, only MP (from p) and MT (from ¬q) are valid. HS, CD and DD are also valid but combine two implications or add a case split.
Valid is not the same as true. A valid argument may have false premises; validity asks only whether the form can carry true premises to a false conclusion. Sound means valid plus all premises true.
Simplification works on ∧ only. From p∨q you may not infer p; that needs a case split, not simplification.
Disjunctive syllogism needs the negation of one disjunct: p∨q with ¬p gives q. From p∨q with p you cannot infer ¬q.
Marks come from the justification column. A line written with no rule name, or with the wrong line numbers, loses credit even when the formula is right.

quiz.q: State modus ponens and write it in symbols.
quiz.a: From p and p→q, infer q. In symbols: p, p→q ⊢ q. Knowing the antecedent true forces the consequent true.

quiz.q: Explain why q, p→q ⊢ p is not valid, using a concrete pair of statements.
quiz.a: Let p be "the power is cut" and q be "the room is dark". The room is dark at night even with power on, so both premises are true while p is false. A true premise set with a false conclusion breaks validity; the form affirms the consequent.

quiz.q: Name the single rule used in each: (a) p∧q ⊢ q, (b) p ⊢ p∨q, (c) p→q, q→r ⊢ p→r, (d) p∨q, ¬q ⊢ p.
quiz.a: (a) simplification, (b) addition, (c) hypothetical syllogism, (d) disjunctive syllogism.

quiz.q: Premises: p→q, q→r, ¬r. Prove ¬p with a numbered proof.
quiz.a: 1. q→r premise. 2. ¬r premise. 3. ¬q by modus tollens on 1, 2. 4. p→q premise. 5. ¬p by modus tollens on 4, 3.

quiz.q: Premises: p∨q, ¬p, q→r. Prove r and justify each line.
quiz.a: 1. p∨q premise. 2. ¬p premise. 3. q by disjunctive syllogism on 1, 2. 4. q→r premise. 5. r by modus ponens on 3, 4. Each line follows by a named rule, so the argument is valid.

quiz.q: A student writes: 1. p→q premise; 2. q premise; 3. p modus ponens on 1, 2. Find the error and repair the argument by changing one premise.
quiz.a: Modus ponens needs the antecedent p, not the consequent q, so line 3 affirms the consequent and the proof is invalid. Change line 2 to p and line 3 to q; or change line 2 to ¬q and conclude ¬p by modus tollens.

beyond: Not for the exam. Resolution, met in 1.9, replaces this whole table with one rule that machines can apply blindly, which is why hardware and software verifiers do not use modus ponens directly. Modern SAT and SMT solvers decide formulas with millions of variables on that idea, and they check contracts inside industrial code. Prolog and Datalog run on resolution over Horn clauses, so a rule like parent(X,Y) :- father(X,Y) is inference theory at work. Search next for "natural deduction", "Horn clause", "SAT solver" and "SMT solver".
